findings.evidence: Wrenford "telo" = wood: misheard: thelo → telo (generation 6) · Wrenford "shubuso" = three: misheard: shubusho → shubuso (generation 34) · Oakhollow "telo" = wood: misheard: thelo → telo (generation 6)

findings.q: Do the words used most change least?
findings.finding: Use vs. replacement rate across meanings: ρ = -0.27, p = 0.405, n = 12. Most used: two (8% replaced per generation), wood (17% replaced per generation), food (3% replaced per generation); least: planks (34%), five (57%).
findings.evidence: Real languages show this (Pagel et al. 2007). n = meanings, so treat as suggestive.

findings.q: Do a few families take over, and does the language narrow with them?
findings.finding: By generation 17, every living agent descends from one founder. Families alive vs. distinct words per meaning across towns: ρ = 0.24, p = 0.099, n = 50.
findings.evidence: Children go to the best-placed parents, so lineages die out: a founder effect, as in population genetics. Caution: families and variety both fall over time, so the correlation may be the language converging, not the families narrowing it.
